whyItExists.problem: When two CSS rules both target the same element and set the same property, the browser must pick one. Without a clear system this would be unpredictable.
whyItExists.solution: The cascade is an algorithm that determines which rule wins. It considers importance, specificity, and source order — in that priority.
whyItExists.whenToUse: You need to understand the cascade when debugging why a style is not applying, when overriding library styles, or when designing a scalable CSS architecture.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: You do not need to think about it explicitly for simple pages with few rules — but understanding it prevents hours of debugging.

explainModes.beginner: CSS has a rule about rules: more specific wins. An ID rule beats a class rule, which beats a tag rule. If specificity ties, the last one written wins.
explainModes.simple: The cascade uses three tiebreakers in order: (1) Is it marked !important? (2) How specific is the selector? (3) Which comes later in the code? First wins that is not a tie, the next tiebreaker decides.
explainModes.standard: Specificity is a three-slot score: (ID count, class+attribute+pseudo-class count, element+pseudo-element count). Inline styles beat all. !important overrides everything except another !important with higher specificity. If specificity ties, the later declaration wins (source order).
explainModes.technical: The cascade algorithm considers: origin (user-agent < author < user), importance (!important reverses origin order), layers (@layer — later layers win), specificity, and source order. CSS Cascade Level 5 adds @layer for explicit layer ordering, giving teams fine control without specificity wars.
explainModes.deepDive: Browsers apply three style origins in cascade order: user-agent (browser defaults), user (OS accessibility settings), and author (the developer's CSS). !important flips the author vs user order, which is why user !important can override author !important — it exists for accessibility. @layer allows declaring multiple named layers; later layers beat earlier ones, and all layered styles beat unlayered styles of equal specificity.

content.text: Every selector has a specificity score written as three numbers (A, B, C):

items: B — number of class, attribute, and pseudo-class selectors (.card, [type], :hover)

content.code:
/*              (A, B, C)  */
p               /* (0, 0, 1) */
.card           /* (0, 1, 0) */
#hero           /* (1, 0, 0) */
p.lead          /* (0, 1, 1) */
#hero .card p   /* (1, 1, 1) */

/* Higher A always beats higher B or C — compare left to right */
#hero  vs  .card.wide.bold  →  #hero wins (1,0,0) > (0,3,0)

content.text: Some CSS properties are inherited by child elements automatically. Typography properties (color, font-size, font-family) inherit. Layout properties (width, margin, padding) do not.
Overusing !important creates a specificity war. Every new override needs another !important. It is a sign that your CSS architecture needs refactoring.

questions.question: Which has the highest specificity?
questions.explanation: #hero has specificity (1,0,0). An ID always beats any number of classes or elements.

questions.question: What happens when two rules have equal specificity?
questions.explanation: When specificity is equal, source order decides — the later declaration wins.

questions.question: CSS properties like color and font-family are inherited by child elements by default.
questions.explanation: Typography properties (color, font-family, font-size, line-height) are inherited. Layout properties (margin, padding, width, border) are not.

faq.q: How do I override a library's styles without !important?
faq.a: Increase your selector's specificity to beat the library's. If the library uses .btn { color: blue; }, your .my-theme .btn { color: red; } has higher specificity and wins without !important.
Cascading means styles can come from multiple sources — browser defaults, external files, inline styles — and the cascade algorithm picks which one applies. The 'cascade' is the priority waterfall.
Yes, except for !important declarations in external stylesheets. Inline styles have specificity (1,0,0,0) — higher than any selector.

examples: Tailwind CSS uses low-specificity utilities and !important sparingly for truly immovable values
Bootstrap's component styles are class-based (0,1,0) so developers can override them with slightly more specific selectors
CSS @layer is used in large apps to ensure utility classes always beat component styles
